lesson_title: Three Questions to Judge a Country
hook_text: If you could ask only three questions to judge how well a country treats its people, what would you ask?
clip_script: In 1990, two economists, one from Pakistan and one from India, said money alone was the wrong way to rank countries. So they asked three questions. Do people live long, healthy lives? Do they get to learn? Do they have enough to live decently? Each answer becomes a score from zero to one. Live to 65 on average? That is about 0,69 for health. Then the three scores are combined so that a country cannot cheat by being rich while its people die young. The result is the Human Development Index. Switzerland and Norway score above 0,95. Somalia and South Sudan, below 0,40. South Africa: about 0,72. That is the high group. But adjust for inequality, and South Africa's score drops more than almost anyone's. One number puts people first. It still cannot show who is left behind.
visual_style: Three question cards labelled health, knowledge and living standard; a dial turning from 0 to 1; a world map shaded in four colours; a South African flag pin on the map with the number 0,72; a bar shrinking when labelled inequality-adjusted.
pacing: Even, with a short pause before the inequality twist.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to see how the HDI is calculated and how to read it critically.
